name: Sam Hazen
title: Chief Executive Officer
overview: Sam Hazen runs the largest hospital company in the country and, from January 2027, the for-profit hospital lobby. HCA booked $75.6 billion in revenue in 2025 and $6.8 billion in net income. Hazen's own 2025 pay was $26.5 million, 420 times the median HCA employee. The company carries the two largest health care fraud settlements in federal history, from 2000 and 2003. In 2026 it is headed to trial in North Carolina over promises it made when it bought Mission Health.
companyRecord: 2025 revenue $75.6 billion, up from $70.6 billion in 2024. Net income $6.8 billion, or $28.33 a share (10-K, 2025).
190 hospitals at December 31, 2025, in 19 states and England. 102 of them are in Florida and Texas, which produce 51% of revenue (10-K, 2025).
189 hospitals and roughly 2,600 ambulatory sites at September 30, 2026 (Q3 2026 release).
Q3 2026: revenue $19.8 billion, net income $1.6 billion. HCA said the shift of patients from exchange coverage to uninsured cut pretax income by $400 million in the quarter.
316,971 employees were paid in 2025. Median total compensation: $62,955 (2026 proxy).
Buybacks: $10 billion authorized in January 2025 and another $10 billion in January 2026. $2.97 billion of stock repurchased in Q3 2026 alone.
November 5, 2026: $6.5 billion of senior notes issued in seven tranches; $1.2 billion of 2027 notes called for redemption.
ownership: Publicly traded. The 10-K treats Hercules Holding II, the 2006 buyout vehicle, and directors and officers as affiliates for float purposes (10-K, 2025).

2006 leveraged buyout: Bain Capital, KKR and Merrill Lynch Global Private Equity with founder Dr. Thomas F. Frist Jr., at $51 a share. Transaction value roughly $33 billion including $11.7 billion of debt (SEC filing, 2006).
Before the 2011 re-IPO, the owners paid themselves $4.257 billion in distributions during 2010 (S-1, 2011).
Two Frist family members, Thomas F. Frist III and William R. Frist, sit on the board (8-K, April 2026).
litigation: December 14, 2000: HCA subsidiaries pled guilty. The company agreed to pay more than $840 million in criminal fines, civil penalties and damages for unlawful billing. DOJ called it the largest government fraud settlement in U.S. history at the time.
June 26, 2003: $631 million in civil penalties for cost report fraud and physician kickbacks, plus a separate $250 million CMS settlement. DOJ put the total recovered from HCA at $1.7 billion.
July 2025: $1.53 million settlement with California, nearly $1.4 million with Colorado and $862,000 with Nevada over training repayment agreements imposed on entry-level nurses.

August 15, 2025: HCA and Mission Health settled the 2022 antitrust suit by Asheville, Brevard, Buncombe County and Madison County. Terms: a $1 million charity care fund and keeping Transylvania Regional Hospital open until at least 2032.
October 2025: final approval of the class settlement over HCA's 2023 data breach, which exposed more than 11 million patients. Up to $5,000 per documented loss; $3.1 million in attorney fees.

July 28, 2026: the North Carolina Business Court sent the Attorney General's suit over the Mission Health purchase agreement to trial. It largely denied HCA summary judgment. The court read the agreement as requiring HCA to actually provide emergency and cancer services.
October 9, 2026: plaintiffs in the 2021 private antitrust class action against Mission Hospital reported an agreement in principle to settle. Terms not public.
Since December 2023, an HCA affiliate has been under investigation by district attorneys in four California counties over waste disposal practices (10-K, 2025).
No new False Claims Act settlement or DOJ action against HCA was found for January 2025 through November 6, 2026.
deals: 2025: $397 million spent on hospital and health care acquisitions, including two hospitals in New Hampshire and Florida. $269 million received from sales, including a California hospital (10-K, 2025).
First nine months of 2026: $942 million spent on nonhospital acquisitions. One Virginia hospital sold for $26 million. Hospital count moved from 190 to 189 (10-Q, Q3 2026).
July 29, 2026: commercial paper program ceiling doubled from $4 billion to $8 billion.
November 5, 2026: $6.5 billion senior notes offering completed.
politicalGiving: Hazen's individual federal contributions since January 2025: not retrieved. The FEC API rate limit blocked every query on November 6, 2026.

developments.text: Annual meeting: Hazen re-elected with 193.7 million votes for and 1.7 million against.
Chief Clinical Officer Dr. Michael Cuffe to step down August 31, 2026.
North Carolina Business Court sends the Attorney General's Mission Hospital case to trial.
Agreement in principle reported in the private Mission Hospital antitrust class action.
FAH elects Hazen Chair for 2027. He was a Director in 2026.
Q3 2026: revenue $19.8 billion, net income $1.6 billion, down 3.9%. $400 million pretax hit from exchange coverage losses.
$6.5 billion of senior notes issued.

redFlags: The FAH chair's company holds the two largest health care fraud settlements in federal history: $840 million in 2000 and $881 million in 2003.
A North Carolina court found HCA's Mission Health purchase agreement requires it to actually provide emergency and cancer services. The state's breach claims go to trial.
Hazen's pay ratio rose from 391:1 to 420:1 in one year while HCA spent $2.97 billion on buybacks in a single quarter.
Three state attorneys general settled with HCA in 2025 over debt-style training repayment contracts imposed on new nurses.
pohRelevance: HCA has 102 hospitals in Florida and Texas, the two states where physician-owned hospitals were growing fastest before the 2010 ban. Every repeal bill in the 119th Congress would open those markets to physician competitors. As FAH chair for 2027, Hazen leads the organization Chip Kahn credited with keeping the ban in place.

name: Saum Sutaria, MD
title: Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
overview: Saum Sutaria spent 18 years at a global consulting firm before joining Tenet as chief operating officer in 2019. He became CEO in September 2021 and chairman in August 2023. His 2025 pay was $43.1 million, 711 times the median Tenet employee, the highest ratio on the FAH board. Tenet owns 51 hospitals and interests in 535 ambulatory surgery centers through USPI, where physicians are the minority partners. FAH elected him chair-elect in October 2026, in line to chair in 2028.

keyStats.label: Surgery centers with USPI interests, Sept. 2026

companyRecord: 2025 net operating revenues $21.3 billion: $16.1 billion hospital operations, $5.2 billion ambulatory care. Net income $1.4 billion (10-K, 2025).
50 hospitals in eight states at December 31, 2025. USPI held interests in 533 ambulatory surgery centers and 26 surgical hospitals in 37 states.
51 hospitals, 535 surgery centers and 25 surgical hospitals at September 30, 2026 (10-Q, Q3 2026).

Q3 2026: net income $1.0 billion, boosted by $646 million of contract termination revenue from the early wind-down of Conifer's CommonSpirit contract. Admissions of patients covered through the ACA exchanges fell, worsening payer mix (10-Q, Q3 2026).
2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance raised to $5.05 billion to $5.20 billion. $1.6 billion of stock repurchased in the first nine months of 2026.
2025 litigation and investigation costs: $64 million, up from $35 million in 2024 (10-K, 2025).
Median employee total compensation in 2025: $60,657 (2026 proxy).
ownership: Publicly traded. No sponsor, REIT master lease or founder control disclosed (10-K, 2025).
USPI is a consolidated Tenet subsidiary. Physicians and health systems hold noncontrolling interests in most facilities: 147 facilities at September 30, 2026.
litigation: August 6, 2003: $54 million to end criminal and civil investigations into unnecessary cardiac procedures at Redding Medical Center. No admission of wrongdoing.
June 29, 2006: more than $900 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations over Medicare outlier payments, kickbacks and coding.
April 10, 2012: $42.75 million over inpatient rehabilitation admissions billed from 2005 to 2007.
October 3, 2016: over $513 million, $368 million civil plus roughly $146 million in criminal forfeiture. Two Atlanta-area subsidiaries pled guilty to paying prenatal clinics for Medicaid referrals.
May 31, 2023: $29.7 million by Detroit Medical Center, Vanguard and Tenet over mid-level practitioner services given to referring physicians below fair market value.
No new False Claims Act settlement or DOJ action against Tenet, USPI or Sutaria was found for January 2025 through November 6, 2026.
deals: 2025: USPI bought controlling interests in 27 surgery centers and one surgical hospital, consolidated nine more and opened six. Purchases of businesses: $308 million (10-K, 2025).
First nine months of 2026: $201 million on business purchases and $583 million buying out noncontrolling interests, most of them physician partners (10-Q, Q3 2026).
January 2026: CommonSpirit agreed to end Conifer's revenue cycle contract early, producing $1.47 billion of termination revenue in the first nine months of 2026.
September 22, 2026: $2.0 billion of 6.250% notes due 2034 issued to retire 2027 and 2028 notes.
November 18, 2025: $1.5 billion of secured notes due 2032 and $750 million of notes due 2033 issued.
politicalGiving: Sutaria's individual federal contributions since January 2025: not retrieved. The FEC API rate limit blocked every query on November 6, 2026.

developments.text: 2026 proxy discloses 2025 pay of $43.1 million and a pay ratio of 711:1.
Annual meeting: Sutaria re-elected 72.3 million to 2.0 million. Say-on-pay passed 62.6 million to 11.8 million.
$2.0 billion senior notes issued.
FAH names Sutaria Chair-Elect for 2027. He was a Director in 2026.
Q3 2026: $1.0 billion net income on $646 million of contract termination revenue; guidance raised.

redFlags: A 711:1 pay ratio, the widest on the FAH board, in a year the company booked $64 million of litigation and investigation costs.
Five federal settlements totaling roughly $1.54 billion, including two guilty pleas by subsidiaries in 2016.
Tenet spent $583 million in nine months of 2026 buying out noncontrolling interests, the physician partners USPI recruits.
Nearly 16% of shareholders voted against Sutaria's pay package in May 2026.
pohRelevance: Tenet's USPI model is the for-profit answer to physician ownership: physicians get a minority stake in a surgery center Tenet controls, never the hospital. A repeal of the POH ban would let those same surgeons own the whole facility and keep the facility fee. Sutaria chairs FAH in 2028, when any year-end 2026 package will be law.

name: David Dill
title: Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
overview: David Dill chaired FAH in 2026 and stays on as immediate past chair and secretary. He became Lifepoint's CEO the day Apollo took the company private in November 2018, collecting a $25.3 million golden parachute in the deal. Apollo's funds own 97% of Lifepoint and draw $9.2 million a year in management fees, per a 2025 Senate Budget Committee report. Lifepoint publishes no financial statements. In June 2026 it bought eight hospitals back from ScionHealth, the Apollo sister company it spun off in 2021.

keyStats.label: Apollo stake in Lifepoint (Senate Budget Committee, 2025)
Annual management fees to Apollo (2025 report)

companyRecord: 68 community hospital campuses, more than 70 rehabilitation and behavioral health hospitals, more than 300 other sites, nearly 59,000 employees (company release, June 16, 2026).
Lifepoint is private. No 2025 revenue, net income, CEO pay or pay ratio is public. The company has filed no SEC periodic reports since delisting on November 16, 2018.

Apollo's RCCH HealthCare Partners merged with LifePoint on November 16, 2018 at $65 a share. Enterprise value roughly $5.6 billion including $2.9 billion of net debt and minority interest (merger announcement, July 23, 2018).
Dill was President and COO before the merger and became CEO at closing (8-K, 2018).
The Senate Budget Committee's bipartisan January 2025 report used Lifepoint's Ottumwa Regional Health Center in Iowa as a case study of underinvestment and declining quality.
No 2025 or 2026 credit rating action on Lifepoint was found.
ownership: Owned by funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management since the 2018 take-private.
Apollo stake roughly 97%; management fees $9.2 million a year (Senate Budget Committee, January 7, 2025).
ScionHealth, also Apollo-backed, was created in December 2021 from Kindred's long-term acute care hospitals plus 18 Lifepoint community hospitals. Lifepoint bought eight of them back on June 2, 2026.
litigation: January 7, 2025: Senate Budget Committee report on private equity hospital ownership, with Lifepoint and Apollo as a case study. Findings: a $9.2 million annual management fee, a 97% Apollo stake, underinvestment and declining quality at Ottumwa.
August 15, 2025: Province Healthcare and eight other Lifepoint entities agreed to pay $9.5 million to settle wage claims by patient-care workers. The case is in Delaware federal court.
September 11, 2025: a Tennessee federal judge denied Lifepoint's motion to dismiss a proposed ERISA class action over 401(k) fees and use of forfeitures.

April 23, 2026: Lifepoint began mailing notices for a February 2026 data breach. It exposed names, addresses, dates of birth and Social Security numbers of contracted vendors' employees. Count not disclosed.
June 2, 2026: Lifepoint sued MultiPlan, Aetna, Cigna, Elevance and other insurers in the Chicago MultiPlan antitrust litigation, alleging a conspiracy to suppress out-of-network reimbursement.
A payment dispute, Legacy Lifepoint Health v. Anthem Health Plans of Kentucky, is in discovery in Kentucky federal court through December 2026.

compensation.total: $25,268,698 golden parachute at the Apollo merger

deals: March 6, 2026: agreement to buy eight acute care hospitals from ScionHealth in Idaho, Mississippi, Tennessee, Texas, West Virginia and Wisconsin. Price not disclosed.
June 2, 2026: the ScionHealth purchase closed. Network now 68 community hospital campuses.
politicalGiving: September 15, 2025: $5,000 to Federation of American Hospitals PAC (FEC).
September 15, 2025: $2,000 to American Hospital Association PAC (FEC).

developments.text: Breach notices mailed for the February 2026 vendor-employee data breach.
Lifepoint completes purchase of eight ScionHealth hospitals.
Lifepoint files antitrust complaint against MultiPlan and major insurers.
CFO Aaron Lewis named President and COO; national CFO search under way.
FAH elects the 2027 slate. Dill moves from Chair to Immediate Past Chair and Secretary.

redFlags: A bipartisan Senate committee found Apollo takes $9.2 million a year in fees from a 97%-owned hospital company. Quality declined at its Iowa case-study hospital.
Dill's $25.3 million parachute was paid by the same buyout that loaded Lifepoint with debt and ended its public reporting.
Lifepoint and ScionHealth, both Apollo companies, have now traded the same hospitals twice, in 2021 and 2026, with no price disclosed either time.
A 2026 breach exposed vendor employees' Social Security numbers. Lifepoint has not said how many.
pohRelevance: Lifepoint's hospitals sit in small markets where a physician-owned competitor would be the only alternative. A 2023 JAMA study found private equity acquisition raised hospital-acquired conditions by 25%, falls by 27% and central line infections by 38%. The POH ban protects that record from competition. Dill chaired the lobby that defends the ban through the year the ban's repeal bills died in committee.

name: Mark Tarr
title: President and Chief Executive Officer
overview: Mark Tarr joined HealthSouth in 1993, ten years before the company's accounting fraud came to light. He has run its successor, Encompass Health, since December 2016. Encompass operates 179 inpatient rehabilitation hospitals and gets 82% of its revenue from Medicare and Medicare Advantage. That makes site-neutral payment reform, which FAH opposes, a direct threat to its model. Tarr was paid $10.3 million in 2025, 203 times the median employee. He is FAH treasurer for a second year.

keyStats.label: Revenue from Medicare and Medicare Advantage, 2025

companyRecord: 2025 net operating revenues $5.94 billion, up 10.5%. Net income $566 million. 173 hospitals in 39 states and Puerto Rico at year end (10-K, 2025).
Payer mix 2025: Medicare 65.4%, Medicare Advantage 16.4%, together roughly 82% of revenue (10-K, 2025).
Q3 2026: revenue $1.61 billion, up 8.9%. Net income $150 million. 179 hospitals. 2026 revenue guidance raised to $6.45 billion to $6.5 billion.
Long-term debt $2.55 billion at September 30, 2026. Quarterly dividend raised to $0.21; buyback authorization raised to $1 billion.
The 10-K cites a MedPAC estimate that a unified post-acute payment system would cut rehabilitation hospital reimbursement by roughly 15%. The company says it cannot verify the methodology.
Tarr: President and CEO since December 29, 2016; joined HealthSouth in 1993; COO from February 2011 (2026 proxy).

HealthSouth's accounting fraud: the SEC charged the company and CEO Richard Scrushy on March 19, 2003 with overstating earnings by at least $1.4 billion. Later tallies put it near $2.7 billion. The company became Encompass Health in January 2018.
ownership: Widely held public company. No controlling holder, private equity sponsor, sovereign stake or REIT master lease.
66 of 174 hospitals were joint ventures as of March 31, 2026, mostly with nonprofit health systems (Q2 2026 slides).
litigation: June 28, 2019: $48 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations. Some rehabilitation facilities gave Medicare inaccurate information to keep their status and admitted ineligible patients. Three whistleblowers shared $12.4 million.
No new DOJ, False Claims Act, state enforcement, data breach or major lawsuit against Encompass Health was found for January 2025 through November 6, 2026.
deals: November 25, 2025: 40-bed joint venture rehabilitation hospital with Vanderbilt Health announced for Lebanon, Tennessee, opening 2028.
June 9, 2026: opened a 40-bed hospital in Loganville, Georgia, the eighth joint venture with Piedmont. Pipeline of 13 hospitals and 606 beds beyond 2026.
Through Q3 2026: four hospitals opened with 189 beds, plus 85 beds added to existing hospitals.
No acquisitions, divestitures or sale-leasebacks were found for 2025 or 2026.
politicalGiving: February 18, 2025: $3,000 to Friends of John Thune and $3,000 to Thune Victory Committee (FEC).
January 6, 2026: $2,500 to Federation of American Hospitals PAC (FEC).

developments.text: 2026 proxy: Tarr's 2025 pay $10.3 million; ratio 203:1.
Q1 2026 call: nurse turnover at its lowest since at least 2012; premium labor spend down 9.4%.
Loganville, Georgia hospital opens.
Dividend raised to $0.21; $1 billion buyback authorization.
FAH re-elects Tarr as Treasurer for 2027.
Q3 2026: revenue up 8.9%, guidance raised, 179 hospitals.

redFlags: Eighty-two percent of revenue comes from Medicare, so every dollar of site-neutral reform FAH blocks is a dollar kept by the FAH treasurer's company.
The 2019 settlement involved telling Medicare inaccurate information to keep facilities qualified for rehabilitation rates.
Tarr spent his career inside HealthSouth, whose earnings were overstated by at least $1.4 billion while he ran its inpatient division.
pohRelevance: Encompass does not compete with physician-owned hospitals on inpatient surgery. Its stake in FAH's agenda is site-neutral payment: MedPAC's unified post-acute system would cut its rates by roughly 15%. As treasurer, Tarr signs off on the budget FAH spends to stop that reform. Physicians who do rehabilitation in office or ASC settings are paid the lower rate today.

sources.label: Encompass Health, Lebanon, Tennessee hospital announcement (Nov. 25, 2025)

name: Marc Miller
nickname: The Heir With 88.9% of the Vote
title: Chief Executive Officer and President
overview: Marc Miller became CEO of Universal Health Services on January 1, 2021, succeeding his father Alan Miller. The founder, now 88, started the company in 1978 and still holds 88.9% of the voting power. UHS runs 388 inpatient behavioral health facilities and 30 acute care hospitals. It paid $122 million in 2020 to settle claims of medically unnecessary psychiatric admissions. Juries have returned verdicts of $535 million and $360 million over abuse at two of its youth facilities. Miller was paid $16.1 million in 2025.

keyStats.label: Voting power held by Alan Miller, 2026 proxy

companyRecord: 2025 net revenues $17.36 billion, up 9.7%. Net income $1.49 billion, up 30% (10-K, 2025).
At September 30, 2026: 30 acute care hospitals, 388 inpatient behavioral health facilities and 169 outpatient and other facilities in the U.S. and U.K.
Q3 2026: revenue $4.73 billion, net income $309 million, diluted EPS $5.22 against $5.86 a year earlier. Miller cited a slower ramp at new hospitals and softer surgical trends.
Total debt rose from $4.69 billion at December 31, 2025 to $5.71 billion at September 30, 2026, after the Talkspace purchase closed in August.
Nine-month 2026 buybacks: 3.915 million shares for $689.6 million.
Miller: CEO and President since January 1, 2021; President since May 2009; 2026 base salary $1,575,000.
ownership: Four share classes. Class B, the public class on the NYSE, carries one-tenth of a vote. Class C carries 100 votes. Class A and C holders elect five of the directors (10-K, 2025).
Alan B. Miller, 88, holds 77.8% of Class A, 100% of Class C and 88.9% of general voting power. He remains Executive Chairman. Marc Miller holds 20.4% of Class A (2026 proxy).
Alan Miller is also Chairman, CEO and President of Universal Health Realty Income Trust, a REIT that leases facilities to UHS.
litigation: July 10, 2020: $117 million by UHS plus $5 million by Turning Point Care Center, $122 million in all. The claims: medically unnecessary inpatient behavioral health admissions and kickbacks from 2006 to 2018. Five-year corporate integrity agreement with an independent monitor. 18 whistleblower cases resolved.

June 12, 2024: Senate Finance Committee staff report, Warehouses of Neglect, on abuse in youth residential treatment facilities run by UHS, Acadia, Devereux and Vivant. UHS called it incomplete and misleading.

March 2024: a jury awarded $535 million against UHS's Pavilion Behavioral Health System in Illinois. The trial court cut punitive damages to $120 million in October 2024. Appeal status after 2025 not found.

September 27, 2024: a Virginia jury awarded $360 million to three former patients of UHS's Cumberland Hospital for Children and Adolescents. Punitive damages were later cut to $1.05 million under Virginia's cap. Roughly 40 more plaintiffs followed.
August 2026: a tentative confidential settlement of all current Cumberland claims. UHS booked a $26 million reserve increase in Q3 2026 and says excess insurance covers a substantial part.

September 26, 2025: a Nevada jury found UHS Delaware interfered with St. Mary's Medical Group physician contracts, awarding $4.7 million compensatory and $500 million punitive. UHS expects Nevada law to cap punitive damages near $14 million.
deals: April 2025: opened Cedar Hill Regional Medical Center GW Health in Washington, D.C., 136 beds, the District's first new full-service hospital in over 25 years.
May 2026: opened the $430 million, 156-bed Alan B. Miller Medical Center in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida.
August 1, 2026: George Washington University moved its Medical Faculty Associates physician practice into Capital Medical Group, a new UHS-controlled nonprofit.
August 17, 2026: completed the purchase of Talkspace for $5.25 a share, roughly $835 million, financed with credit agreement borrowings.
politicalGiving: No contributions by Marc Miller were found in an FEC search by employer for January 2025 through November 2026. A name-and-state search hit the API rate limit and was not completed.
Alan B. Miller gave $99 to the National Republican Senatorial Committee on October 17, 2025 (FEC).

developments.text: 2026 proxy: Miller's 2025 pay $16.1 million; ratio 283:1; Alan Miller holds 88.9% of voting power.
Definitive agreement with George Washington University on the Medical Faculty Associates physician practice.
Capital Medical Group transaction finalized; UHS takes financial responsibility for GW physician practice operations.
Talkspace acquisition closes.
Tentative settlement of the Cumberland Hospital abuse litigation.
FAH 2027 slate lists Miller as Director. He was Immediate Past Chair in 2026.
Q3 2026: EPS $5.22 against $5.86; debt $5.71 billion.

redFlags: Public shareholders hold one-tenth of a vote per share. The founder's family controls 88.9% of the vote, and the founder also runs the REIT that is UHS's landlord.
Two juries found UHS youth psychiatric facilities liable for patient abuse, with initial awards of $535 million and $360 million.
A Nevada jury found UHS interfered with physician contracts at a competing medical group and awarded $500 million in punitive damages.
The 2020 settlement covered 12 years of admitting psychiatric patients who did not need to be admitted.
pohRelevance: UHS took over George Washington University's physician practice in 2026, the academic version of the employment model the POH ban protects. Its acute care hospitals in Nevada, Texas and Florida face the same physician competitors as HCA's. The Nevada verdict shows what UHS does when physicians try to leave: a jury found it interfered with their contracts.

name: Kevin Hammons
title: President and Chief Executive Officer
overview: Kevin Hammons spent 28 years at Community Health Systems, the last five as chief financial officer, before becoming CEO on December 10, 2025. His job is to shrink the company. CHS has sold or exited 15 hospitals since the start of 2025 and is down to 59 in 12 states, from 69 a year earlier. Debt is $9.6 billion. Q3 2026 brought a $86 million loss and a 10.7% drop in revenue. Hammons told investors payer mix and acuity did not develop as expected.
companyRecord: 2025 net operating revenues $12.5 billion, down 1.2%. Net income $509 million, helped by divestiture gains, after a $516 million loss in 2024. 69 hospitals in 14 states at year end (10-K, 2025).

Q3 2026: revenue $2.76 billion, down 10.7%. Net loss $86 million. Nine-month loss $74 million. 59 hospitals in 12 states at October 28, 2026. Cash on hand $155 million, down from $260 million at year end.
Total debt $10.4 billion at December 31, 2025 and $9.59 billion at September 30, 2026, down from $11.45 billion a year earlier.
2025 divestitures: four hospitals and majority interests in three others, with 2024 revenue near $792 million, for net proceeds over $1.0 billion.
Roughly 57,000 employees at December 31, 2025 (2026 proxy).
Hammons: interim CEO from October 1, 2025; CEO and director since December 10, 2025; CFO 2020 to 2025. He joined CHS in 1997 after ten years at a Big Four audit firm.
ownership: Widely held public company. No controlling stockholder, private equity sponsor or sovereign stake.
CHS bought Health Management Associates on January 27, 2014 for roughly $7.6 billion including assumed debt. HMA's conduct produced the 2018 DOJ settlement.
litigation: September 25, 2018: $262 million to resolve the HMA matters: a $216 million civil False Claims Act settlement plus $35 million in criminal penalties. Carlisle HMA, former operator of a Pennsylvania hospital, agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy. The allegations: improperly admitting emergency patients as inpatients, and kickbacks.
September 23, 2020: $2.3 million to HHS over the 2014 cyberattack that exposed 6.1 million people's health information, plus a two-year corrective action plan.
October 2020: $5 million to 28 state attorneys general over the same breach.

May 2021: CNN found CHS hospitals had filed at least 19,000 lawsuits against patients for unpaid bills since March 13, 2020. CHS said its policy is not to sue patients earning under 200% of the federal poverty level.
No new DOJ, False Claims Act, state enforcement action or data breach involving CHS was found for January 2025 through November 6, 2026.

compensation.total: Not applicable (Hammons was CFO; CEO Tim Hingtgen: $7,629,625)

deals: 2025: sold Lake Norman Regional Medical Center (NC) to Duke for $284 million. Also sold two ShorePoint hospitals (FL) to AdventHealth, 80% of Cedar Park Regional (TX) to Ascension, and half-interests in two Mississippi hospitals.
December 1, 2025: sold Northwest Health Physicians' Specialty Hospital (AR) to Washington Regional. Labcorp bought the outreach lab business.
February 1, 2026: sold 80% of Tennova Healthcare Clarksville to Vanderbilt for $623 million. Sold three Pennsylvania hospitals to Tenor Health Foundation for $33 million cash plus a $15 million note.
April 1, 2026: sold Crestwood Medical Center (Huntsville, AL) to Huntsville Hospital Health System for $459 million.
June 1, 2026: sold four Northwest Arkansas hospitals to Freeman Health System for $110 million.
One more hospital left the count between September 30 and October 28, 2026. Details not found.
politicalGiving: November 10, 2025: $5,000 to Federation of American Hospitals PAC (FEC).
March 7, 2026: $1,000 to Trump National Committee JFC and $775 to Never Surrender, Inc. (FEC).
May 1 and June 30, 2026: $500 and $1,033.06 to Joe Mitchell for Congress (FEC).

2026 proxy: Hammons's 2025 pay $4.8 million; ratio 60:1; base salary $1.25 million.
Four Arkansas hospitals sold to Freeman Health System for $110 million.

A 2014 breach exposed 6.1 million people and cost $7.3 million in federal and state settlements.
The company is selling hospitals to pay down $9.6 billion of debt while losing money on the ones it keeps.
pohRelevance: CHS is the clearest case of what the POH ban protects: a highly leveraged chain that cannot compete and is selling hospitals to survive. Its buyers in 2025 and 2026 were nonprofit systems, Duke, Vanderbilt, AdventHealth and Ascension, never physicians, because physicians cannot own a Medicare hospital. Lifting the ban would create a second class of buyer for the hospitals CHS still has to sell.

name: Prem Reddy, MD
title: Founder, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
overview: Prem Reddy, a cardiologist, built Prime Healthcare from one California hospital in 1994 into a 55-hospital chain in 15 states by buying distressed hospitals. Prime and Reddy have paid $103.75 million in three False Claims Act settlements since 2018. Reddy paid $5.0 million of it from his own pocket. In 2025 Prime bought eight Ascension hospitals in Illinois for $375 million, then cut pediatric, trauma and obstetric services. Two senators and a House member have demanded answers. Prime is private and publishes no financial statements.

keyStats.label: Paid personally by Reddy in two of them
Price of eight Ascension Illinois hospitals, 2025

companyRecord: 55 hospitals in 15 states and more than 360 outpatient locations. The nonprofit Prime Healthcare Foundation owns 21 of them (Prime, 2026).
Prime is private. No revenue or net income figure is published.
September 2024: $1.5 billion of senior secured notes due 2029 issued to retire 2025 notes and fund acquisitions.
2025 ratings: Fitch raised the secured notes to B+ and Moody's raised the corporate rating to B2. S&P affirmed with a positive outlook (Prime release, August 2025).
Franciscan Health Olympia Fields, bought May 8, 2026, was Prime's 55th hospital and ninth in Illinois.
Leadership page lists Sunitha Reddy, Ravi Reddy and Seetha Reddy among the executives. Relationships are not stated.
ownership: Privately held and founder-led. Prem Reddy is Founder, Chairman and CEO (Prime leadership page).

Two rails: the for-profit Prime Healthcare Services, Inc., which issues the bonds, and the nonprofit Prime Healthcare Foundation. The Foundation owns 21 hospitals and bought Central Maine Healthcare in February 2026.
litigation: August 3, 2018: Prime and Reddy agreed to pay $65 million. The claims: 14 California hospitals admitted patients who needed only outpatient care and upcoded diagnoses. Reddy paid $3.25 million personally. A corporate integrity agreement followed.
February 14, 2019: $1.25 million over unnecessary short inpatient stays and upcoding at Roxborough Memorial and Lower Bucks hospitals in Pennsylvania. Reddy's personal share not found.

July 19, 2021: $37.5 million with DOJ and the California Attorney General. Prime paid $33.7 million, Reddy $1.775 million, and a cardiologist $2 million. The claims: kickbacks tied to buying the cardiologist's practice to steer referrals, billing under a physician with revoked privileges, and inflated implant invoices. Five-year corporate integrity agreement for Prime and Reddy.
May 20, 2025: Senators Durbin and Duckworth demanded answers on service cuts at the eight former Ascension Illinois hospitals. Prime replied it was losing nearly $200 million a year there.
May 2026: the Illinois Nurses Association and Aurora's mayor criticized unit shutdowns at Prime hospitals. They backed HB 4757, which would let the state review board deny acquisitions.
September 4, 2026: Prime announced it would suspend labor and delivery at three Illinois hospitals. Rep. Lauren Underwood called it a pattern of revenue-focused decisions and broken promises.
No new False Claims Act settlement or DOJ action against Prime or Reddy was found for January 2025 through November 6, 2026.
deals: March 1, 2025: completed the purchase of eight Ascension Illinois hospitals for $375 million, pledging $250 million of investment. A ninth, Ascension St. Elizabeth, closed before the deal did.
February 16, 2026: the Prime Healthcare Foundation took over Central Maine Healthcare, three hospitals, by membership substitution. It assumed the debts and pledged $150 million over five years.
May 8, 2026: Olympia Fields purchase closed after an 8 to 0 Illinois review board vote. Becker's reports $101 million in private bonds plus an $18 million reserve fund.

September 2026: labor and delivery suspended at Saint Joseph's (Joliet), Mercy (Aurora) and Resurrection (Chicago). Prime cited fewer than one delivery a day. A $1 million maternal care grant to two other hospitals was announced the same month.
politicalGiving: Reddy's individual federal contributions since January 2025: not retrieved. One FEC query reported 14 records before the API rate limit closed; the records were not captured.
A Prime Healthcare PAC could not be identified in FEC records on November 6, 2026.

redFlags: Three False Claims Act settlements in four years, two of them with Reddy paying personally, and two corporate integrity agreements.
The 2021 settlement included billing under a physician whose privileges had been revoked and kickbacks to buy a cardiologist's referrals.
Within 18 months of buying eight Illinois hospitals, Prime suspended obstetrics at three of them and drew letters from two senators and a congresswoman.
A nonprofit foundation controlled by a for-profit founder now owns 21 hospitals, including three in Maine acquired by taking over the nonprofit's membership.
pohRelevance: Prime's model is buying hospitals that nonprofits want to shed, then cutting the services that lose money. A physician-owned competitor in Joliet or Aurora could offer the obstetrics Prime dropped. The ban means the only alternative buyer for a failing hospital is another chain. Reddy, himself a physician, sits on the board that keeps other physicians from owning.

name: Dave Caspers
title: President and Chief Executive Officer
overview: Dave Caspers became Ardent's CEO on June 2, 2026, when the board removed Marty Bonick, FAH's chair-elect at the time. Caspers spent his career in retail health: Target, seven years at Banner Health, Walmart's in-store clinics, then a pool supply chain. He joined Ardent as COO in March 2025. In October 2026 the board reclassified Bonick's exit as a firing for cause over undisclosed outside pay. Ardent is controlled by the Zell family's EGI, with Abu Dhabi's Pure Health holding 21% and its landlord Ventas holding 6.5%. He took Bonick's FAH seat.
companyRecord: 2025 revenue $6.32 billion, up 6.0%. Net income $136 million, down from $210 million (10-K, 2025).
30 acute care hospitals and more than 280 sites in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, New Jersey, Idaho and Kansas. The UT Health East Texas joint venture is 19.4% of revenue.
Q2 2026, Caspers's first quarter: revenue down 1.4%, adjusted EBITDA down 32.3%, net income $16.9 million against $73.0 million a year earlier. Net income guidance cut.
Q3 2026: revenue $1.62 billion, up 3.1%. Net income $44.5 million. Adjusted EBITDA guidance raised to $500 million to $535 million. Capital spending cut.
Related-party rent to Ventas, which also owns 6.5% of the stock: $152.9 million in 2025, $149.2 million in 2024 (10-K, 2025).
Stock listed July 18, 2024 at $16.00. It closed 2025 at $8.83 (2026 proxy).
Workforce reduction severance: $10.3 million in 2025, $10.4 million in 2024, $12.4 million in 2023 (8-K, September 2026).

Caspers: COO from March 31, 2025. Before Ardent he was Chief Stores Officer at Leslie's, the pool supply retailer, 2023 to 2025. Earlier: Walmart Health, 2022 to 2023; Banner Health, 2015 to 2022; Target before that (8-K, June 2026).
ownership: EGI-AM Investments, an affiliate of the Zell family's Equity Group Investments, holds 54.0% and can name a majority of directors and the chairman (2026 proxy).
Pure Health Capital Americas, an affiliate of Abu Dhabi's Pure Health Holding, holds 21.1%.
ALH Holdings, a subsidiary of the REIT Ventas, holds 6.5% and can name one director. Ardent leases ten hospitals and 18 medical office buildings from Ventas.
litigation: January 7, 2026: securities class action Postiwala v. Ardent Health in Tennessee federal court against the company, Bonick and the CFO. Class period July 18, 2024 to November 12, 2025. It centers on accounts receivable reserving. Motion to dismiss filed September 28, 2026.
February 26, 2026: stockholder derivative suit Thompson v. Sotir against current officers and directors.

October 19, 2026: the board found Bonick had not fully disclosed compensation from third parties. It reclassified his departure as for cause. Roughly $4.5 million of unpaid severance was stopped and his unvested performance shares cancelled (8-K, October 23, 2026).
2025: a $475,000 retirement plan fee settlement received final court approval. The November 2023 cybersecurity class action was settled in 2025.
No DOJ, False Claims Act or state enforcement action against Ardent was found for January 2025 through November 6, 2026. Nothing names Caspers personally.

deals: January 2025: 18 urgent care clinics in New Mexico and Oklahoma bought from NextCare.

September 29, 2026: agreement to sell Ardent's 70.5% of the Topeka St. Francis campus to the University of Kansas Hospital Authority for $58.4 million, ending a 2017 joint venture. Caspers called the hospital not the right long-term fit.
politicalGiving: February 16, 2026: $750 to Ardent's corporate PAC, listed as Chief Operations Officer (FEC). No other contribution found since January 2024.

developments.text: Appointed President and CEO, succeeding Marty Bonick. Guidance reaffirmed; the CFO cited second-quarter volume softness.
CFO at an investor conference: the CEO change was proactive; the board wants operational execution and margins.
Q2 2026: adjusted EBITDA down 32.3%; net income guidance cut; cost program raised to $70 million.
Agreement to exit the Topeka St. Francis joint venture at $58.4 million.
Named a Director on FAH's 2027 board, taking the Ardent seat.
Board reclassifies Bonick's departure as for cause; $4.5 million of severance stopped.
Q3 2026: revenue up 3.1%, net income $44.5 million, EBITDA guidance raised, capital spending cut.
Q3 call: salaries and benefits down 4%; the CFO said about half the surgical volume decline was intentional.

redFlags: The FAH seat passed from an executive the company later said was fired for cause to a CEO with no hospital-company CEO experience.
Ardent's second-largest shareholder is a sovereign-linked Abu Dhabi company; its third-largest is its own landlord, which collected $152.9 million in rent in 2025.
A securities class action alleges the company misstated its receivables from the IPO through November 2025.
Caspers has made no public policy statement. Ardent's positions on Medicaid, site-neutral and exchange coverage come from its CFO.
pohRelevance: Ardent's hospitals are in Texas, Oklahoma and New Mexico, where physician-owned hospitals were strongest before 2010. Its Texas joint venture with UT Health is 19.4% of revenue. A rural POH bill like H.R. 2191 would open exactly those markets. Caspers brings a retail operator's view to a board whose job is to keep physician competitors out.

name: Doug Shirley
title: Chief Executive Officer
sector: Long-term acute care, private equity owned
overview: Doug Shirley is a career hospital finance executive who became ScionHealth's CEO on June 10, 2026 after 14 months as its CFO. ScionHealth is the Apollo-owned company spun out of Lifepoint in 2021 to hold Kindred's long-term acute care hospitals. Moody's rates it deep in junk. It closed three hospitals in 2025 and sold eight more to Lifepoint in June 2026. It now depends on its landlord Ventas for a $300 million loan at 10.7%. Shirley replaced Rob Jay on the FAH board. He has no public policy record.

Annual rent on 23 Kindred hospitals from May 2025

companyRecord: 62 long-term acute care hospitals under the Kindred, Cornerstone and Solara brands, plus six community hospital campuses, in 23 states. More than 16,000 employees (company page, unchanged since April 2025).
Private; no revenue, net income or debt figure is published. A 2023 statement filed in Indiana lists a $450 million term loan due 2028.
Formed December 2021 when Apollo-owned Lifepoint bought Kindred and spun the long-term hospitals plus 18 community hospitals into a new 79-hospital company.

Moody's cut the corporate rating to Caa2 in December 2023. In January 2025 it added a limited default marker after a distressed exchange and cited weak liquidity and an unsustainable capital structure.
February 2025: closures announced for Kindred Chicago Lakeshore, Kindred Sycamore and Kindred Bay Area in Tampa, with more than 300 layoffs. Occupancy at the Chicago hospitals was near a third.
June 2, 2026: eight community hospitals in six states sold to Lifepoint, the Apollo sister company that spun them off. Price not disclosed.

Shirley: CFO from April 8, 2025. Before that he was CFO of PathGroup and National Group and revenue cycle head at Surgery Partners. Earlier he was CFO of Cooper Health System in New Jersey from 2009 and a PwC health care advisory director in Nashville. Earlier senior roles at Ardent Health Services.
ownership: Owned by Apollo Global Management funds since 2021. The percentage and fund are not public.
Ventas, the REIT landlord, holds warrants for 9.9% of the equity of a Kindred parent, exercisable until September 2034 (Ventas 10-K, 2025).
Ventas is also a secured lender since June 2026: a $300 million six-year interest-only loan at 10.7%. Kindred's rent and loans are guaranteed by the corporate parent.
litigation: February 2023: Cornerstone Healthcare Group paid $21.6 million to settle False Claims Act allegations over Medicare billing from 2012 to 2018. ScionHealth bought Cornerstone in January 2023, after the conduct period.

September 2026: union members picketed Kindred Hospital San Diego and Kindred Hospital Bay Area in San Leandro over staffing and equipment. The union cites 129 state complaints at San Diego since 2023.
No 2025 or 2026 lawsuit, DOJ matter, attorney general action or bankruptcy involving ScionHealth was found in web searches.
deals: September 16, 2024: Ventas bought five Kindred hospitals for $189 million and leased them back at $16 million a year. Rent on 23 other Kindred hospitals reset from $109 million to $80 million from May 1, 2025. Ventas received warrants for 9.9% of the equity.
February 2025: three hospital closures announced; all closed by April 30, 2025.
March 6 to June 2, 2026: eight community hospitals sold to Lifepoint. ScionHealth keeps its long-term hospitals and six community campuses.
June 2026: all Kindred leases combined into one master lease running to April 30, 2039. Ventas lends $300 million at 10.7% in a refinancing meant to reduce debt.
politicalGiving: No federal contribution by Shirley was found for January 2024 through November 2026 (FEC searches by name in Kentucky and Tennessee).
ScionHealth's corporate PAC raised $88,353 and gave $62,000 to other committees in the 2025-26 cycle through October 14, 2026 (FEC).

redFlags: A company rated Caa2 with a limited default marker now has a seat on the hospital lobby's board. Its landlord is also its lender and a warrant holder.
Three hospitals closed in 2025 and eight were sold in 2026 to an affiliate under the same private equity owner, with no price disclosed.
Shirley came to ScionHealth from Ardent Health Services, the company of fellow new director Dave Caspers, and before that from Surgery Partners.
No public statement by Shirley on any policy question was found.
pohRelevance: ScionHealth's long-term acute care hospitals do not compete with physician-owned surgical hospitals. Its stake in FAH is Medicare payment. The long-term hospital rate, the 25-day stay rule and the site-neutral criteria decide which patients it can bill at the higher rate. Those are the same payment distinctions FAH defends against physician offices. Shirley's seat is a creditor's seat: the money that keeps ScionHealth solvent is Medicare's.
